title: Skill Can Make It Good; Dedication Makes It Timeless.
description: A branding project came in, and I had my first meeting with the founder, Mr Raghav Kohli, and the promoter, Mr Deepak Sahni. Deepak and I had worked together before on several brands, so there was already a shared understanding of how a brand story can help and inspire me.

blocks.heading: A branding project came in, and I had my first meeting with the founder, *Mr Raghav Kohli*, and the promoter, *Mr Deepak Sahni*. Deepak and I had worked together before on several brands, so there was already a shared understanding of how a brand story can help and inspire me.
The brand was a Japanese matcha tea brand. They wanted to call it HIKARI.

The story was not simply about flavour or authenticity, even though the product was made with pure Japanese ingredients. *It wasn't about replacing a habit, or even about how matcha could become part of a luxury lifestyle.*
It may have been all of those things, but what stayed with me from our conversation was something else.
HIKARI was about meeting your *better self.*
It was about self-discovery, about self-care, and about completing a journey of knowing yourself. A bridge between you and your real, unadulterated self. A journey back to your core.

As Raghav was explaining all of this, my mind was flying through Japanese blossoms and still lakes, with the sound of a mystic flute somewhere in the distance.

I saw a bridge.

A *simple bridge* stretching across a calm lake. It was taking me towards the other side, while its *reflection was bringing me back to where I had started.* Somehow, the journey forward became a journey back to myself, to my core.

And that stayed with me.
We started the design process as we usually do. We explored a few ideas, filtered them, questioned them, and gradually came out with three distinct directions.

There was no real clear indication or inclination towards one particular direction from our side. The client's team, however, liked one direction the most and wanted us to take that ahead.

So we did.

After several iterations, as you can see below, the identity reached a stage where we felt confident sharing it with the client's team.

*They loved the whole brand deck.*

The conversations then naturally moved towards the real application goals: the sizes of the boxes, packaging, applications and the marketing tone of voice.

Which was when the visual of the bridge came back to my mind.

I started thinking along those lines again. At the same time, I was going through the final logo files, and I saw the bridge.

Not there.

Not yet.

But the possibility of it.

This is an interesting stage in any branding project. When the logo is finalised, when nobody is asking any more questions about it, and when the work has essentially reached its goal, you can either stop there—or ask yourself if there is still something more that the identity can hold.

We were trying to cross the limits of a good logo in the quest to make it a memorable one.

*So we took one last step.*

Sumit Singh from my team, who had worked on the identity and brought the logo to this stage with remarkable care, immediately understood what I was trying to achieve. Together, we explored one final refinement.

The change was subtle.

You can see the difference.

But more importantly, you can feel it.

This difference was not something anyone had asked for. It was not part of the brief. It did not add to the fees, nor did it create another milestone or an additional effort list.

What it added was something far more valuable: job satisfaction of a supreme level.

It was the result of the conviction that had been shown to us. The result of a responsibility felt well enough to strive even after the goal had been achieved.

And perhaps, most importantly, it was the result of the faith between Client and Designer.

Good design satisfies the brief.

But meaningful design continues asking questions even after the brief has been answered.

Skill is what allows us to solve a problem.

Dedication is what persuades us to keep looking after the solution, even after it has already been found.

Perhaps that is what makes certain pieces of design timeless.

Not because they were difficult to create, but because someone cared enough to take one last step.
